name: mem_fs
description: Start MemProcFS on a memory image for the length of one call, do one thing with the file tree it mounts, and stop it: the mount is released when the call returns, so nothing later can read it, unless the clean-up itself failed (an engine that cannot be ended, an unmount helper that does not answer): the answer then says so in a named cleanup problem and the mount may still be there; what survives is the files an export wrote and the engine's own stdout and stderr, kept as files (mode 0600) beside the mount. SENSITIVE: memory can hold anything the machine held (command lines, environments, keys, process pages), so mode text and mode export, which write content, and mode list with write_values, which writes the original names, run only as a job run as secret output and only with write_values: true, and write only to $OUT/mem_fs (mode 0600, created exclusively, never over an existing file); this manifest declares secret_output for write_values, so the harness seals the job, and the tool refuses as JSON, before MemProcFS starts, when SECRET_OUTPUT is not 1 or the call is not a job. The manifest of exports is appended to by every call of the job (a second export in the same job adds its rows). secret_values.contains_secret_values is true when the job's output holds values from this call or an earlier one (earlier_calls_in_this_job_wrote_values says which), also in a call that asked for none; the manifest is the record. The byte count and sha256 of an item are of the bytes the system accepted, so a disk that fills leaves a count, a digest and a file that agree, and the status says how many bytes are on disk. Every directory the tool creates under $OUT/mem_fs is mode 0700. The answer is a locator (virtual path, output file, size, status per item) with no content and no digest of content; sizes and sha256 are in $OUT/mem_fs/export-manifest.jsonl. Each exported file also has a ranges file, JSON Lines under $OUT/mem_fs/%ranges/, named <output name>%.json (items[].ranges: its path, size and sha256, and a count for each class): kind read (the bytes copied), unavailable (the mount gave no bytes there: the read that failed, which can span up to 1 MiB because the failing page within it is not known, or a file that ended before the size the mount reports; the item is then failed or partial, never complete), not_copied (the copy did not reach it: it was stopped, bounded, could not write, or stopped at the first read error and did not try the rest), and zero_filled (whole aligned 4096-byte pages in which every copied byte is 0), then a summary row; a ranges file without a summary row was cut, and one that could not be written whole makes the answer not complete (ranges.problems). Zero-filled means the bytes are zeros: MemProcFS fills a page it cannot read with zeros and a file can hold real zeros, so it is not proof that data is missing. The copy stops at the first read error and does not try the pages after it. A file that gives more bytes than the mount reports is partial. After a stop, the file being copied is listed with its manifest row and a ranges file that ends in its summary row; if the copy did not end within its grace period the answer says so in unfinished and names the file. Names the engine lists and lines it prints come from the capture and are judged before they are shown: a name is shown when it has no invisible character, no component over 128 characters and no 16-character-or-longer run of letters and digits that looks random, and no deny-list or backstop rule reads it as a secret; otherwise it, or the span, is a placeholder with its length (name_withheld), listed after the plain names in an order new every call; with write_values the original names go to $OUT/mem_fs/names.jsonl. Withholding is by shape: a plain password, a pronounceable passphrase or any name under 16 characters is printed. Measured residuals of the name boundary, on planted keys (1,000 per cell; a name alone, then inside proc_<k>.exe, <k>.dll and 1234-<k>), as the share printed whole: base64 and base62 keys 0 to 0.6 per cent alone and up to 2.9 per cent in a process-name context (24 base62 characters 2.9, 20 bytes of base64 1.2, 20 base62 characters 2.4); in an engine line, which a failure shows and which has no allow-list, base64 keys of 16 to 32 bytes 0 to 18 per cent, base62 keys of 20 to 32 characters 10 to 61, a 24-character base36 key 48 to 65 and a base64 key holding / 37 to 40. The prefixes of the AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe (sk_live_, rk_live_, pk_live_, whsec_), GitLab and SendGrid keys, JWTs, 40-digit hexadecimal keys and user-info were not printed in 3,400 plants per shape. Not read at all, and printed in every cell tried: UUID-shaped secrets, 16-digit hexadecimal secrets, tokens split by . or : into pieces under 16 characters, word passwords and passphrases (100 per cent); and printed at the rates given: 14-character policy passwords (67 to 100 per cent), base32 seeds (43 to 46), licence keys of five groups of five characters (18 to 20) and 12-character fragments of a bcrypt hash (28 to 31). A name that matters is read in a job run as secret output, with write_values. A failure shows at most the first 20 lines of the engine's output, judged as text; the logs are the files named, each the first 1 MiB of its stream (logs.*_dropped_bytes counts what the engine wrote after that: it is read and discarded, so a verbose engine can neither fill the disk nor stop on a full pipe). mode list shows names, kinds and sizes of a directory, no content. mode export copies the named virtual files byte for byte (never as text, never inside JSON); mode text writes one file only if it is UTF-8 text with no NUL byte and within max_bytes_per_path, and refuses anything else instead of decoding it with replacements. A file over max_bytes_per_path is not exported and is counted; an item that could not be exported says why and complete is false; the counts add up to the paths requested, and a path the worker did not reach is counted not_attempted. Output names write every character outside a small safe set as %XX of its bytes, so two different names never share an output file. One deadline (timeout_seconds, 2 to 480) holds over startup, reads and export; stopping the engine and unmounting after it has its own bounded wait (at most 100 s where /proc is read, 112 s where the process table falls back to ps, which the clean-up runs twice with 10 s each and 2 s to end it; a check of the mount that has to be ended at the deadline adds 2 s before it), so the call stays inside the tool's 600 s (480 + 2 + 112 = 594). What the engine started and daemonised before the clean-up listing, or forked after it, may still hold the pipes the tool made for the engine: on Linux the clean-up finds the processes that hold them through /proc/<pid>/fd (pipe:[inode]), ends each one with SIGTERM and then SIGKILL (2 s each) after checking its start time and its pipe again just before the signal (through a pidfd where the kernel has one), and names each in clean_up.pipe_holders (pid and how it ended; a holder that could not be ended is a cleanup problem). It never signals this tool, pid 1 or an ancestor of this tool, and the kill set is never wider than the processes that hold one of those pipes. The search takes 2 s at most (search_complete says whether it finished); a process that closed its copies of the pipes is not found, and off Linux, or where /proc cannot be read, nothing is searched, so a process the engine daemonised may outlive the call. No stat of the mount is made by the tool itself: the readiness check at startup and the checks of whether the mount is still there are made by a short child process that is killed at its time limit, so a FUSE server that does not answer cannot hold the tool past those bounds. At startup a mount that does not answer ends the call as not ready, at the deadline; in the clean-up it is named as still there and not answering (cleanup_problems lists every trouble of the clean-up, also when an earlier problem is the one named). The unmount helper is killed after 12 s and waited for 2 s more; a child or helper that is still not reaped then is named with its pid and left running. A FUSE mount that does not answer before the engine is started (a stale mount at the path) is not covered. A failure names the phase (startup, read, export, cleanup); the engine is then stopped and unmounted, and a stop or an unmount that fails is named as the cleanup phase (the mount may then remain). A signal (SIGTERM, SIGINT, SIGHUP) ends it with one JSON answer (status interrupted, exit 128 plus the signal) after the engine is stopped and the mount released; rows already kept in the results file are named in partial_results; the engine also ends with the tool on Linux. A signal that arrives once the engine is stopped, while the results file is being placed and the answer written, is held until the answer is out (stdout never holds two documents, and no file is half-placed). A stop that arrives before the interpreter has run the tool's first lines (tens of milliseconds at the start of a process, longer on a loaded machine) ends it with no answer; no engine had been started and nothing had been written then. A virtual path that resolves outside the mount (a link) is refused for that item, and a link loop or any other failure is that item's status; the other items go on. Whether MemProcFS contacts a symbol server is governed by the job's network policy (a job has no network unless it asks for the run's allowlist); this tool passes MemProcFS no flag about it, and the pinned binary's behaviour in that respect was not verified in this review. It needs MemProcFS, /dev/fuse the process can open and fusermount3 or fusermount, which a sandbox may not provide: the answer says which of these the host has (blocked_by names what is missing). It mounts, exports and measures nothing else: it does not say what a file means, that a region is complete or that a page was resident, and which virtual paths exist depends on the MemProcFS version and the image (list first). A name, a path, a URL or a message that quotes a credential is withheld with the identifier-shaped strings, from version 17: a value given to a password, token, secret or cookie name (password=..., Pwd=..., a Cookie header), a Name/Value pair in text whose Name is a credential (a number, an array or a long Value too, and the NewValue after an OldValue), a -Password style switch, the argument of ConvertTo-SecureString, curl -u user:pass, mysql -uUSER -pSECRET, a bcrypt hash and the known token families; the text is replaced by a marker that holds only its length. Before, only identifier-shaped strings (tokens, key ids, user-info) were withheld, so these were printed. Known gaps: a pair whose Value is an array nested in another or longer than 4,096 characters, a crypt hash that is not bcrypt, and a secret that has neither a credential name nor a token shape.

mount.description: Where to mount it: a directory under your own work/<your id>/ (in a job, under $OUT); it must be empty. The engine's two log files are written beside it and kept

mode.description: list (default): names, kinds and sizes. text: one UTF-8 text file written to $OUT/mem_fs. export: the files in paths, byte for byte, to $OUT/mem_fs. text and export need write_values and a job run as secret output

list.description: A path inside the mount: the directory to list (default: the mount's root) or, with mode text, the one file to write out

paths.description: With mode export: the virtual files to copy (at most 1000), relative paths inside the mount

write_values.description: Write memory content to files (default false). Required by text and export; with mode list it writes the original names of the entries whose name was withheld or changed to $OUT/mem_fs/names.jsonl. Refused unless the tool runs as a job, which the harness runs as secret output because the manifest declares it; the answer never carries content

max_bytes_per_path.description: Do not export a file larger than this (default 4294967296); it is counted and named, not cut. Raise it to export a larger file

limit.description: Entries or items shown inline (default 200, at most 5000: a larger value is clamped and the answer says limit_clamped_to); all are counted, and when there are more the whole list is written as JSON Lines and named in complete_results

timeout_seconds.description: One deadline for startup, reads and export (default 300, 2 to 480); stopping the engine and unmounting after it has its own bounded wait of at most 100 s (112 s where the process table falls back to ps)
